title: test-0044-SCI-BIO-HEREDITY
passage: In the remote islands of the Galapagos, scientists recently observed a unique population of finches. Unlike the common belief that species evolve because they 'need' to change to survive, these birds changed simply due to random variations in their DNA that happened to be advantageous during a drought. Some birds were born with slightly larger beaks, not because their parents exercised their jaw muscles, but due to genetic shuffling. These larger-beaked birds survived better, passing their genes to the next generation. Interestingly, researchers noted that having a dominant gene for beak size does not mean it will immediately become the most common trait in the population. Furthermore, while we often think of evolution as a ladder toward perfection, these finches are not 'better' than their ancestors; they are simply adapted to their current environment. It is also a common myth that gametes carry two alleles for every gene; in reality, these reproductive cells contain only one allele, ensuring that when fertilization occurs, the offspring receives a complete set. This process of inheritance is purely statistical, meaning a pair of parents with a specific genetic makeup will not produce an exact 3:1 ratio of offspring in every small family group. Evolution remains a slow, non-purposeful process of survival, not a directed journey toward a perfect organism.
summary: Unlike the common belief that species evolve because they "need" to change to survive, these birds changed simply because of random variations in their DNA that happened to be advantageous during a drought. Yes, it's also a common myth that gametes carry two alleles for every gene — but in reality, these reproductive cells only have one allele, so when they get fertilized, the offspring gets a complete set.
